claims.text: Localized laser surface melting of HfNbTaTiZr will create an ultrafine-grained surface layer.
The laser-melted surface layer will contain a high density of sub-grain boundaries.
Sub-grain boundaries in the treated layer will act as irradiation-defect sinks.
Laser-induced microstructural refinement will reduce the accumulation of irradiation-induced defects.
The treatment will reduce radiation-induced surface swelling or hardness increase by approximately 20% relative to untreated samples.
Conventionally cast or forged refractory high-entropy alloy is in a coarse-grained initial state.
The intervention remelts an approximately 1 mm thick surface layer in an inert atmosphere.
Rapid solidification after laser melting will produce an ultrafine-grained microstructure.
The treated near-surface region will contain high densities of dislocation networks.
The increased sink density will capture and annihilate mobile radiation-induced point defects.
Capturing and annihilating point defects will prevent formation of defect clusters responsible for irradiation swelling and hardening.
Localized surface treatment will leave the bulk mechanical properties intact.
The proposed benefit will occur primarily within an approximately 1 mm deep near-surface region.
The proposed benefit is expected under irradiation at 600–800 °C.
Hardness, swelling, defect density, and treated-layer microstructure can be compared between laser-treated and untreated samples under identical irradiation conditions.
